strengths: Novel approach combining meta-learning with test-time gradient descent on memory tokens; clean WRITE/READ decomposition with explicit optimization objective
Comprehensive synthetic benchmark (KV-retrieval) demonstrates clear advantages over forward-only writing, with consistent scaling across gradient steps
Well-motivated problem setup (context removal), clear presentation with excellent figures, and thorough appendices including computational analysis and efficient double-backward implementation

Strong technical execution: proper meta-learning framework (MAML), gradient descent formulation is sound, and ablation showing first-order approximations fail demonstrates appropriate use of second-order optimization
Honest treatment of limitations: discusses training overhead, when test-time compute is worthwhile (Section D), and provides code for reproducibility
weaknesses: Weak transfer to natural language tasks contradicts main contribution claims: SQuAD reaches 54.9% vs 64.2% for GPT-2 (~10% gap); bAbI QA3 achieves 79.3% vs 92.3% for ARMT; language modeling underperforms at 2.92 CE vs 2.72 for GPT-2, undermining task-agnostic reconstruction objective

Significant scalability concerns not adequately addressed: (1) all experiments on small models (4-layer to 160M parameters), (2) no analysis of training time overhead with double-backward through attention, (3) unclear feasibility on modern 7B+ models where second-order gradients become prohibitive

Limited practical applicability due to: (1) artificial context removal constraint (real applications like RAG have context access), (2) computational break-even requires ~60 queries per context (Equation 11, Figure 6), (3) large WRITE overhead limits single-query scenarios

Questionable baseline comparisons: RMT appears unexpectedly weak (19.3% on 32-pair KV-retrieval), fair comparison complicated by different memory architectures (per-layer vs single memory state), and limited comparison to other recent gradient-based compression methods (KV-Distill, ICAE, etc.)

Insufficient analysis of core design choices and assumptions: (1) no ablation on separate WRITE/READ heads or learned projections despite implementation details in Appendix B, (2) 'few-step regime' overstated as Figure 4 shows continued improvements far beyond training steps (K=30), (3) task-specific memory sizes (8 vs 32 tokens) lack justification

strengths: Clear technical contribution with sound methodology: gradient-based WRITE operations are more expressive than forward-only alternatives, properly implemented with MAML-style meta-learning
Convincing synthetic experiments on KV-retrieval with clean benchmark: Table 1 demonstrates K=1 outperforms forward-only methods; Figure 4 shows consistent scaling with more gradient steps

Thorough experimental evaluation: multiple datasets (synthetic + NLP), extensive ablations (memory-K tradeoffs, input vs per-layer memory, comparisons to TTT-Linear/LaCT), analysis of learned representations (selective value retention)
Excellent reproducibility: code available, minimal code example, detailed implementation details (Appendix B), documented custom optimizations (Appendix C), complete hyperparameter specifications

Honest treatment of limitations: clearly analyzes when GradMem is compute-efficient (break-even analysis), discusses applicability constraints, acknowledges reconstruction objective may not be optimal for all tasks

Good technical soundness: proper second-order meta-learning with thorough ablations showing importance (w/o 2nd-order ablation in Table 1), fair comparison to RMT baseline with identical architecture/memory size
weaknesses: Limited practical impact on NLP tasks: Table 2 shows mixed results with GradMem matching or underperforming RMT; notably on QA3 GradMem significantly underperforms (80.0% vs 87.9% for RMT), and language modeling improvements are marginal (2.92 vs 2.91)

Significant computational training overhead: requires custom double-backward kernels through attention, curriculum learning needed for stability, second-order meta-learning is expensive and critical (Table 1 ablation), limiting scalability and adoption

Restricted applicability: method only beneficial when context reused multiple times (break-even can require tens to hundreds of queries), requires c >> m, thus limited to specific scenarios; not a general-purpose compression method

Insufficient analysis of failure modes: no investigation of why GradMem underperforms on QA3 despite task-agnostic objective; limited testing on diverse domains beyond synthetic+NLP; no analysis of behavior on very long contexts (>1024 tokens)

Design choices lack principled justification: Appendix J shows per-layer memory with 8× more parameters outperforms input-level memory, suggesting memory parameterization choice driven more by parameter budget than principled design; reconstruction loss selection acknowledged as suboptimal but minimally explored

Limited evidence of scalability to large models: Appendix I tests only 1B-3B models on very short spans (8-64 tokens) with LoRA adapters; main results on 100M scale; scalability to 7B+ models not demonstrated
